question: A 22-year-old medical student reviews carbohydrate structures and is asked to identify which monosaccharide is a ketose rather than an aldose. Which of the following best fits that classification?
cited_learning_objective: Define aldose and ketose and list important examples of each

options.text: Fructose
options.rationale: Fructose is listed in the lecture as an important ketose; ketoses have a carbonyl at an internal carbon rather than an aldehyde at C1.

options.text: Glucose
options.rationale: Glucose is an aldose with an aldehyde at the carbonyl carbon; it would be correct only if the carbonyl were at an internal carbon as in a ketose.

options.text: Galactose
options.rationale: Galactose is an aldose and an epimer of glucose at C-4; it would be correct only if its carbonyl were a ketone rather than an aldehyde.

options.text: Glyceraldehyde
options.rationale: Glyceraldehyde is an aldose (an aldotriose); it would be correct only if it were dihydroxyacetone, the ketotriose.

options.text: Mannose
options.rationale: Mannose is an aldose and a C-2 epimer of glucose; it would be correct only if its carbonyl were a ketone.

question: Which structural relationship describes two hexoses that differ only by the orientation of the hydroxyl group at carbon 4?
cited_learning_objective: Define enantiomers, epimers, and isomers in the context of carbohydrates and give an example of each

options.text: C-4 epimers
options.rationale: The lecture defines epimers as sugars differing at only one chiral carbon and gives glucose and galactose as C-4 epimers.

options.text: Enantiomers
options.rationale: Enantiomers are mirror-image stereoisomers differing at all chiral centers; this would be correct only if the molecules were non-superimposable mirror images.

options.text: Constitutional isomers
options.rationale: Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity of atoms; this would be correct only if the two hexoses had different bond connectivities, not just one chiral center.

options.text: Anomers
options.rationale: Anomers differ at the anomeric carbon (α vs β) formed during cyclization; this would be correct only if the difference were at C-1 after ring closure.

options.text: Diastereomers
options.rationale: Diastereomers differ at one or more but not all chiral centers; while epimers are a subset of diastereomers, the specific term for a single-carbon difference at C-4 is 'C-4 epimers.'

question: A student draws D- and L-forms of a triose and asks how the D/L designation is determined. Which rule from the lecture correctly identifies the basis for D versus L nomenclature?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the basic structure of carbohydrates and D vs L enantiomers

options.text: Orientation of the hydroxyl on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl
options.rationale: Lecture states D/L is assigned by the position of the OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl; D has the OH to the right in Fischer projection.

options.text: Configuration at the anomeric carbon after cyclization
options.rationale: Anomeric configuration (α/β) is determined after ring formation at C-1; it would be correct only if asking about anomers rather than D/L stereochemistry.

options.text: Absolute R/S stereochemical assignment at every chiral center
options.rationale: R/S is a different stereochemical system; D/L specifically uses the reference carbon farthest from the carbonyl and would be correct only if R/S matched that orientation.

options.text: Position of the carbonyl group in the linear chain
options.rationale: Position of the carbonyl distinguishes aldose versus ketose, not D versus L; this would be correct only if the question asked aldose/ketose classification.

options.text: Number of carbons in the backbone
options.rationale: Carbon count defines triose/tetrose/pentose/hexose categories; it would be correct only if D/L designation depended on chain length, which it does not.

question: Which glycosidic linkage connects the two monosaccharides in lactose and which intestinal enzyme hydrolyzes it?
cited_learning_objective: List the monosaccharides and glycosidic bonds involved for each of the physiologically important disaccharides as well as where they can be found

options.text: β(1→4) linkage hydrolyzed by lactase
options.rationale: Lecture specifies lactose is galactose–glucose linked by a β(1→4) bond and is cleaved by lactase on small intestinal cells.

options.text: α(1→2) linkage hydrolyzed by sucrase
options.rationale: α(1→2) is the sucrose linkage (glucose–fructose) cleaved by sucrase; it would be correct only if the disaccharide were sucrose.

options.text: α(1→4) linkage hydrolyzed by maltase
options.rationale: α(1→4) is the maltose linkage (glucose–glucose) cleaved by maltase; it would be correct only if the disaccharide were maltose.

options.text: β(1→3) linkage hydrolyzed by cellulase
options.rationale: Cellulase cleaves β(1→4) cellulose linkages, not β(1→3); this would be correct only if cellulose had β(1→3) bonds and humans produced cellulase.

options.text: α(1→6) linkage hydrolyzed by isomaltase
options.rationale: α(1→6) is a branch point linkage in glycogen and starch; isomaltase can act on some α(1→6) linkages, but this is not the lactose bond.

question: A patient with lactase deficiency consumes milk and develops watery diarrhea and bloating. According to the lecture, which mechanism best explains the diarrhea?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the enzyme deficiency and findings in lactose intolerance

options.text: Unabsorbed disaccharide increases luminal osmolarity drawing water into the colon
options.rationale: Lecture explains excess lactose exerts an osmotic effect, drawing water into the large intestine and causing watery diarrhea.

options.text: Bacterial overgrowth consumes lactose and reduces luminal osmolarity
options.rationale: Bacterial fermentation produces gas and acids but does not reduce osmolarity; this would be correct only if fermentation lowered osmotic load, which it does not.

options.text: Lactase deficiency increases bile acid secretion causing secretory diarrhea
options.rationale: Bile acid–mediated secretory diarrhea is unrelated to lactase deficiency; it would be correct only if bile acid malabsorption were present.

options.text: Pancreatic enzyme insufficiency prevents lactose digestion leading to steatorrhea
options.rationale: Pancreatic insufficiency affects fat digestion, not lactose; this would be correct only if pancreatic enzymes were deficient and fats were malabsorbed.

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of enterocytes reduces water absorption causing osmotic diarrhea
options.rationale: Autoimmune enterocyte loss can cause malabsorption but is not the mechanism described for lactase deficiency; it would be correct only if enterocyte destruction were documented.

question: Which polysaccharide is the primary storage form of glucose in animals and how is it structurally different from plant amylopectin according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast glycogen, starch, and cellulose, and discuss the glycosidic bonds involved

options.text: Glycogen; more frequent α(1→6) branching every 8–10 residues
options.rationale: Lecture states glycogen is animal storage with α(1→4) chains and α(1→6) branches occurring every 8–10 residues, more frequent than amylopectin.

options.text: Amylose; linear α(1→4) chains with no branching
options.rationale: Amylose is plant starch with linear α(1→4) linkages and no branches; it would be correct only if asking about unbranched plant starch, not animal storage.

options.text: Cellulose; β(1→4) linkages forming unbranched structural fibers
options.rationale: Cellulose is structural with β(1→4) bonds and no branching; it would be correct only if the question asked about structural plant polysaccharides rather than storage.

options.text: Amylopectin; α(1→6) branching every 8–10 residues similar to glycogen
options.rationale: Amylopectin branches every 20–30 residues per the lecture; it would be correct only if its branching frequency matched glycogen's.

options.text: Chitin; N-acetylglucosamine polymers with β(1→4) bonds
options.rationale: Chitin is a structural polymer of N-acetylglucosamine with β(1→4) bonds in fungi and arthropods; it would be correct only if the question asked about structural polysaccharides outside plants/animals.

question: A researcher incubates a sample of plant cell wall material with an enzyme that specifically cleaves β(1→4) glucose linkages. Which enzyme from the lecture would perform this reaction and what would be the expected product?
cited_learning_objective: Compare and contrast glycogen, starch, and cellulose, and discuss the glycosidic bonds involved

options.text: Cellulase; glucose monomers from cellulose
options.rationale: Lecture notes that cellulase breaks β(1→4) linkages in cellulose; cleavage yields glucose units from the cellulose polymer.

options.text: Amylase; maltose from amylose
options.rationale: Amylase cleaves α(1→4) bonds in starch producing maltose and maltotriose; it would be correct only if the substrate were starch, not cellulose.

options.text: Lysozyme; N-acetylmuramic acid fragments from peptidoglycan
options.rationale: Lysozyme cleaves β(1→4) bonds between N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid in bacterial cell walls; it would be correct only for peptidoglycan, not plant cellulose.

options.text: Lactase; galactose and glucose from lactose
options.rationale: Lactase hydrolyzes β(1→4) lactose into galactose and glucose; it would be correct only if the substrate were lactose, not cellulose.

options.text: Isomaltase; glucose from α(1→6) branch points
options.rationale: Isomaltase acts on α(1→6) linkages at branch points in glycogen/starch; it would be correct only if the enzyme targeted α(1→6) bonds rather than β(1→4).

question: A clinician explains why dietary fiber improves stool bulk and regularity. Based on the lecture, which statement best describes the biochemical reason fiber resists human digestion?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the role that cellulose plays in the health benefits of dietary fiber

options.text: Humans lack cellulase and cannot hydrolyze β(1→4) cellulose bonds
options.rationale: Lecture explicitly states humans lack cellulase, so cellulose with β(1→4) linkages is indigestible and acts as bulking fiber.

options.text: Humans lack amylase and cannot hydrolyze α(1→4) starch bonds
options.rationale: Humans produce amylase and can digest α(1→4) bonds in starch; this would be correct only if amylase were absent.

options.text: Cellulose is composed of fructose polymers resistant to intestinal enzymes
options.rationale: Cellulose is glucose-based, not fructose; this would be correct only if cellulose were a fructan resistant to digestion.

options.text: Dietary fiber is rapidly absorbed in the small intestine preventing fermentation
options.rationale: Fiber is not absorbed and often reaches the colon where fermentation occurs; this would be correct only if fiber were absorbable.

options.text: Lactase deficiency causes accumulation of cellulose in the gut
options.rationale: Lactase acts on lactose, not cellulose; this would be correct only if lactase hydrolyzed β(1→4) cellulose bonds, which it does not.

question: A patient with a suspected mucopolysaccharide storage disorder has accumulation of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. According to the lecture, which pair of enzymes when deficient correspond to Hurler and Hunter syndromes respectively?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the enzyme deficiency and findings in mucopolysaccharidoses

options.text: α-L-iduronidase deficiency and iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency
options.rationale: Lecture lists Hurler as α-L-iduronidase deficiency and Hunter as iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, both causing heparan and dermatan sulfate accumulation.

options.text: β-glucuronidase deficiency and arylsulfatase B deficiency
options.rationale: These enzymes are involved in other mucopolysaccharidoses; this would be correct only if the syndromes in question were those specific disorders.

options.text: Hexosaminidase A deficiency and sphingomyelinase deficiency
options.rationale: Hexosaminidase A and sphingomyelinase deficiencies cause Tay–Sachs and Niemann–Pick respectively, not Hurler/Hunter; it would be correct only if the storage products matched those diseases.

options.text: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency and α-L-iduronidase deficiency
options.rationale: This reverses the enzyme–syndrome pairing; it would be correct only if the syndromes were swapped between enzymes.

options.text: Arylsulfatase A deficiency and galactocerebrosidase deficiency
options.rationale: These deficiencies cause metachromatic leukodystrophy and Krabbe disease respectively, not Hurler/Hunter; it would be correct only if the clinical features matched those leukodystrophies.

question: A pathology slide shows bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan. Which repeating disaccharide pair and linkage described in the lecture composes this structure and is a target for lysozyme?
cited_learning_objective: Describe amino sugars and bacterial cell wall composition

options.text: N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid linked by β(1→4)
options.rationale: Lecture states peptidoglycan is alternating GlcNAc and MurNAc linked by β(1→4), and lysozyme cleaves this bond.

options.text: Glucose and galactose linked by α(1→4)
options.rationale: Glucose–galactose α(1→4) is not peptidoglycan; it would be correct only if bacterial walls used those monosaccharides and α linkages.

options.text: N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid linked by β(1→3)
options.rationale: This describes some glycosaminoglycan linkages, not peptidoglycan; it would be correct only if peptidoglycan used glucuronic acid and β(1→3) bonds.

options.text: N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose linked by β(1→4)
options.rationale: This combination appears in other glycoconjugates; it would be correct only if bacterial peptidoglycan used GalNAc instead of GlcNAc.

options.text: Fructose polymers linked by β(2→1)
options.rationale: Fructan β(2→1) linkages are not components of peptidoglycan; it would be correct only if bacterial walls were composed of fructose polymers.

question: A clinician asks which mucopolysaccharide is abundant in synovial fluid and serves as a lubricant in joint cavities. Which molecule from the lecture fits this description?
cited_learning_objective: List the functions of mucopolysaccharides and identify hyaluronic acid

options.text: Hyaluronate (hyaluronic acid)
options.rationale: Lecture states hyaluronic acid is found in connective tissues and synovial fluid and serves as a lubricant in joint cavities.

options.text: Heparin
options.rationale: Heparin is an anticoagulant component of ECM and cell surfaces; it would be correct only if the question asked about anticoagulant glycosaminoglycans.

options.text: Chondroitin sulfate
options.rationale: Chondroitin sulfate is a cartilage component but hyaluronate is the primary synovial lubricant; it would be correct only if the focus were cartilage structure.

options.text: Keratan sulfate
options.rationale: Keratan sulfate is found in cornea and tendons; it would be correct only if the question targeted corneal extracellular matrix.

options.text: Dermatan sulfate
options.rationale: Dermatan sulfate is present in skin and blood vessels; it would be correct only if the question asked about skin ECM components.

question: A lab report shows a glycoprotein with carbohydrate attached to an asparagine residue. According to the lecture, which type of linkage is this and which amino acid side chain is involved?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss proteoglycan linkages and N-glycosidic bonds

options.text: N-glycosidic linkage to asparagine side chain amide nitrogen
options.rationale: Lecture explains N-glycosidic bonds attach carbohydrates to the amide nitrogen of asparagine side chains.

options.text: O-glycosidic linkage to serine side chain hydroxyl oxygen
options.rationale: O-glycosidic bonds attach to serine/threonine hydroxyls; this would be correct only if the sugar were linked to Ser/Thr rather than Asn.

options.text: N-glycosidic linkage to lysine side chain amine nitrogen
options.rationale: Lysine has a primary amine but N-glycosylation in proteins occurs on asparagine; it would be correct only if lysine were the canonical N-linked site.

options.text: O-glycosidic linkage to tyrosine phenolic oxygen
options.rationale: Tyrosine O-glycosylation is rare; lecture specifies Ser/Thr for O-glycosidic bonds, so this would be correct only in exceptional cases.

options.text: Thioether linkage to cysteine sulfur atom
options.rationale: Thioether glycosylation is not described in the lecture; it would be correct only if an uncommon sulfur-linked glycosylation were present.

question: A patient’s red blood cell membrane is analyzed and shows the H substance oligosaccharide but lacks an additional terminal sugar. Based on the lecture, which blood type does this pattern represent?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the structure of substance H and the A, B, and O blood types

options.text: Type O blood
options.rationale: Lecture states type O contains only the H substance without additional terminal sugars, producing no A or B antigens.

options.text: Type A blood
options.rationale: Type A has N-acetylgalactosamine added to the H substance; it would be correct only if that terminal sugar were present.

options.text: Type B blood
options.rationale: Type B has galactose added to the H substance; it would be correct only if galactose were attached.

options.text: Bombay phenotype
options.rationale: Bombay phenotype lacks H substance entirely and cannot express A or B; it would be correct only if H substance were absent, not present alone.

options.text: Type AB blood
options.rationale: Type AB expresses both A and B terminal sugars on H substance; it would be correct only if both N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose were attached.

question: A patient with influenza infection has viral hemagglutinin that binds a specific sugar on host cells. Which carbohydrate mentioned in the lecture serves as that viral receptor?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the role of sialic acid in viral entry and immunology

options.text: Sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid)
options.rationale: Lecture notes influenza hemagglutinin binds sialic acid residues on target tissues, facilitating viral entry.

options.text: N-acetylglucosamine
options.rationale: GlcNAc is a common glycan component but influenza HA specifically recognizes sialic acid; it would be correct only if HA targeted GlcNAc.

options.text: Galactose
options.rationale: Galactose is part of many glycans but HA binding is mediated by sialic acid; it would be correct only if the virus bound terminal galactose instead.

options.text: Fructose
options.rationale: Fructose is not a typical terminal receptor for influenza HA; it would be correct only if HA had affinity for fructose residues.

options.text: N-acetylmuramic acid
options.rationale: Muramic acid is a bacterial cell wall component, not a host cell surface receptor for influenza; it would be correct only in a bacterial context.

question: A student is quizzed on disaccharide composition: which pair of monosaccharides composes sucrose and what is the glycosidic linkage between them as taught in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: List the monosaccharides and glycosidic bonds involved for each of the physiologically important disaccharides

options.text: Glucose and fructose joined by an α(1→2) bond
options.rationale: Lecture states sucrose is glucose–fructose linked by an α(1→2) glycosidic bond.

options.text: Glucose and galactose joined by a β(1→4) bond
options.rationale: This describes lactose (galactose–glucose β(1→4)); it would be correct only if the disaccharide were lactose.

options.text: Two glucose molecules joined by an α(1→4) bond
options.rationale: This describes maltose (glucose–glucose α(1→4)); it would be correct only if the disaccharide were maltose.

options.text: Glucose and fructose joined by a β(1→4) bond
options.rationale: Sucrose has an α(1→2) linkage, not β(1→4); it would be correct only if the anomeric configurations and carbons matched that bond.

options.text: Galactose and fructose joined by an α(1→6) bond
options.rationale: This combination and linkage are not the physiological sucrose structure; it would be correct only if sucrose composition were different.

question: A patient presents with chronic constipation and is counseled to increase intake of plant-based fiber. Which lecture-based statement best explains how this intervention affects bowel function?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the role that cellulose plays in the health benefits of dietary fiber

options.text: Insoluble cellulose increases stool bulk because humans cannot digest β(1→4) bonds
options.rationale: Lecture indicates indigestible cellulose (β(1→4) linkages) acts as a bulking agent, normalizing bowel movements.

options.text: Soluble cellulose is absorbed and increases colonic water reabsorption
options.rationale: Cellulose is insoluble and not absorbed; this would be correct only if the fiber were a soluble, absorbable carbohydrate that increased water reabsorption.

options.text: Dietary cellulose is hydrolyzed by human amylase producing short-chain fatty acids
options.rationale: Amylase acts on α(1→4) starch, not cellulose; fermentation by colonic bacteria can produce SCFAs, but human enzymes do not hydrolyze cellulose.

options.text: Cellulose reduces stool bulk by binding bile acids and preventing water retention
options.rationale: Binding bile acids may affect cholesterol but does not reduce stool bulk; this would be correct only if cellulose decreased luminal water content.

options.text: Increased cellulose intake stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion improving digestion
options.rationale: Cellulose does not stimulate pancreatic enzymes to improve digestion; it would be correct only if fiber directly increased pancreatic exocrine activity.

question: A clinician asks which enzyme activity would be absent in a patient who cannot cleave cellulose in their diet. Based on the lecture, which enzyme is missing?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the role that cellulose plays in the health benefits of dietary fiber

options.text: Cellulase
options.rationale: Lecture explicitly states humans lack cellulase, the enzyme that breaks β(1→4) linkages in cellulose.

options.text: Amylase
options.rationale: Amylase digests α(1→4) starch bonds; absence of amylase would impair starch digestion, not cellulose cleavage.

options.text: Lactase
options.rationale: Lactase hydrolyzes lactose β(1→4) bonds between galactose and glucose; its absence causes lactose intolerance, not inability to digest cellulose.

options.text: Sucrase
options.rationale: Sucrase cleaves sucrose α(1→2) bonds; lack of sucrase affects sucrose digestion, not cellulose.

options.text: Lysozyme
options.rationale: Lysozyme cleaves peptidoglycan β(1→4) bonds in bacterial cell walls, not plant cellulose; it would be correct only if peptidoglycan were the substrate.

question: A patient’s stool sample shows increased bacterial fermentation products after lactose ingestion. Which lecture-described process explains the gas and cramping experienced by this patient?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the enzyme deficiency and findings in lactose intolerance

options.text: Unabsorbed lactose is fermented by colonic bacteria producing gas and acids
options.rationale: Lecture explains lactase deficiency leads to excess lactose in the gut, which bacteria ferment to gas and acids causing bloating and cramping.

options.text: Lactose is converted to bile salts increasing intestinal motility
options.rationale: Lactose does not convert to bile salts; this would be correct only if lactose metabolism produced bile acids affecting motility.

options.text: Pancreatic lipase digests lactose producing free fatty acids that irritate colon
options.rationale: Pancreatic lipase acts on fats, not lactose; this would be correct only if lipase hydrolyzed disaccharides.

options.text: Intestinal brush-border peptidases degrade lactose causing osmotic diarrhea
options.rationale: Peptidases act on peptides, not lactose; this would be correct only if brush-border peptidases hydrolyzed disaccharides.

options.text: Excess lactose increases colonic absorption of water leading to constipation
options.rationale: Excess lactose increases luminal osmolarity and draws water into the colon causing diarrhea, not constipation; this would be correct only if lactose promoted water absorption.

question: A biochemistry lab demonstrates phosphorylation of glucose upon cellular entry. According to the lecture, what is the primary purpose of intracellular phosphorylation of free monosaccharides like glucose?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss phosphorylation of sugars and its cellular consequences

options.text: Trap sugar inside the cell by preventing transporter re-export
options.rationale: Lecture explains phosphorylation (e.g., glucose → G6P) locks sugar inside the cell because transporters cannot bind phosphorylated glucose, maintaining the gradient.

options.text: Make the sugar membrane-permeable for mitochondrial uptake
options.rationale: Phosphorylation actually prevents membrane transport rather than facilitating it; it would be correct only if phosphorylation increased membrane permeability.

options.text: Convert glucose into a storage polymer directly
options.rationale: Phosphorylation is the first step in glycolysis and metabolism, not direct polymerization; it would be correct only if G6P were immediately polymerized into glycogen without further steps.

options.text: Neutralize the sugar's charge to allow diffusion
options.rationale: Phosphate adds negative charge rather than neutralizing it; this would be correct only if phosphorylation reduced charge to permit diffusion.

options.text: Signal for immediate export from the cell via vesicles
options.rationale: Phosphorylation prevents export by transporters; it would be correct only if phosphorylation targeted sugars for vesicular export, which the lecture does not state.

question: A pharmacology student asks which class of glycosides includes digitalis and what cardiac effect is produced by these compounds as described in the lecture.
cited_learning_objective: Describe glycosides and cardiac glycoside effects

options.text: Cardiac glycosides; inhibit Na+/K+ ATPase increasing contractility
options.rationale: Lecture describes digitalis (a cardiac glycoside) inhibiting Na+/K+ pumps, which increases contractility and decreases heart rate.

options.text: Anthraquinone glycosides; stimulate Na+/K+ ATPase decreasing contractility
options.rationale: Anthraquinone glycosides are laxatives and do not stimulate Na+/K+ ATPase; this would be correct only if they had the opposite cardiac effect.

options.text: Saponin glycosides; block calcium channels reducing contractility
options.rationale: Saponins have different biological effects and are not described as Na+/K+ ATPase inhibitors; it would be correct only if they blocked calcium channels as stated.

options.text: Flavonoid glycosides; increase heart rate by β-adrenergic stimulation
options.rationale: Flavonoids are not cardiac glycosides acting on Na+/K+ ATPase; this would be correct only if they acted as β-agonists, which the lecture does not indicate.

options.text: Steroid glycosides; activate Na+/K+ ATPase increasing heart rate
options.rationale: Digitalis is a steroid-like cardiac glycoside but it inhibits, not activates, Na+/K+ ATPase and increases contractility while decreasing heart rate; this option is incorrect in mechanism and effect.

question: A patient with a mucin-rich secretion is sampled. The carbohydrate portion is predominantly N-acetylgalactosamine attached to serine residues. According to the lecture, which linkage type and proteoglycan classification does this represent?
cited_learning_objective: Differentiate proteoglycan types and O-glycosidic linkages in mucins

options.text: O-glycosidic linkage; mucoprotein (mucin)
options.rationale: Lecture states mucins have >10% carbohydrate, often N-acetylgalactosamine, attached via O-glycosidic bonds to Ser/Thr, classifying them as mucoproteins.

options.text: N-glycosidic linkage; glycoprotein
options.rationale: N-glycosidic bonds attach to asparagine and are typical of glycoproteins with <10% carbohydrate; this would be correct only if the sugar were on Asn.

options.text: Thioether linkage; proteoglycan core protein
options.rationale: Thioether linkages to cysteine are not described for proteoglycans; it would be correct only if an uncommon sulfur linkage were present.

options.text: O-glycosidic linkage; glycosaminoglycan
options.rationale: Glycosaminoglycans are long repeating disaccharides often attached to proteins as proteoglycans, but mucins specifically are mucoproteins with O-linked GalNAc; this would be correct only if the carbohydrate were a GAG.

options.text: N-glycosidic linkage; mucopolysaccharide
options.rationale: Mucopolysaccharides (GAGs) are not typically N-linked to Asn in mucins; this would be correct only if the GAG were N-linked, which is not the lecture description.

question: A student is asked which monosaccharide is a common component of the H substance oligosaccharide on red blood cells and is present in the lecture’s depiction of blood group antigens. Which monosaccharide is part of the H core?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the structure of substance H and the A, B, and O blood types

options.text: N-acetylglucosamine
options.rationale: Lecture indicates the H substance contains N-acetylglucosamine, galactose, and fucose as its core three-sugar oligosaccharide.

options.text: N-acetylgalactosamine
options.rationale: N-acetylgalactosamine is the terminal sugar added to form the A antigen, not part of the minimal H core; it would be correct only if the H substance already had the A modification.

options.text: Fructose
options.rationale: Fructose is not part of the H substance core as depicted in the lecture; it would be correct only if the oligosaccharide composition included fructose, which it does not.

options.text: Glucose
options.rationale: Glucose is not listed as a component of the H substance core in the lecture; it would be correct only if the core sugars were different.

options.text: N-acetylneuraminic acid
options.rationale: Sialic acid (NANA) is a terminal residue in some glycans but is not the core H substance sugar listed; it would be correct only if sialylation defined the H core.

question: A patient with suspected Hunter syndrome lacks corneal clouding but shows hepatosplenomegaly and behavioral changes. Based on the lecture, which inheritance pattern and enzyme deficiency best match this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Identify clinical features and inheritance of Hunter syndrome

options.text: X-linked recessive iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency
options.rationale: Lecture describes Hunter syndrome as X-linked due to iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, with milder Hurler features and no corneal clouding.

options.text: Autosomal recessive α-L-iduronidase deficiency
options.rationale: α-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome (AR) with corneal clouding; it would be correct only if the patient had Hurler features.

options.text: Autosomal dominant heparanase deficiency
options.rationale: Heparanase deficiency and AD inheritance are not described in the lecture; it would be correct only if a different enzyme and inheritance matched Hunter.

options.text: X-linked recessive α-L-iduronidase deficiency
options.rationale: α-L-iduronidase deficiency is AR Hurler, not X-linked Hunter; this would be correct only if inheritance were misassigned.

options.text: Autosomal recessive iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency
options.rationale: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency is X-linked Hunter, not AR; it would be correct only if inheritance were autosomal recessive.

question: A patient’s bacterial infection is treated with a drug that enhances lysozyme activity. According to the lecture, lysozyme cleaves which bond in bacterial cell walls and between which two sugar residues?
cited_learning_objective: Describe peptidoglycan structure and lysozyme cleavage site

options.text: β(1→4) bond between N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid
options.rationale: Lecture indicates lysozyme cleaves the β(1→4) linkage between GlcNAc and MurNAc in peptidoglycan.

options.text: α(1→4) bond between glucose and glucose in starch
options.rationale: α(1→4) bonds are in starch and cleaved by amylase, not lysozyme; it would be correct only if lysozyme targeted starch.

options.text: β(1→3) bond between glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine
options.rationale: β(1→3) bonds occur in some GAGs, not peptidoglycan; it would be correct only if lysozyme targeted GAGs.

options.text: α(1→6) bond at glycogen branch points
options.rationale: α(1→6) branch points are cleaved by debranching enzymes/isomaltase, not lysozyme; it would be correct only if lysozyme acted on glycogen.

options.text: β(1→4) bond between glucose and galactose in lactose
options.rationale: Lactose β(1→4) is cleaved by lactase, not lysozyme; it would be correct only if lysozyme hydrolyzed lactose.

question: A patient with a genetic inability to add N-acetylgalactosamine to the H substance would lack which blood group antigen according to the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Explain how terminal sugar additions determine A and B antigens

options.text: A antigen
options.rationale: Lecture states the A antigen is formed by adding N-acetylgalactosamine to the H substance; inability to add it prevents A antigen expression.

options.text: B antigen
options.rationale: B antigen requires addition of galactose, not N-acetylgalactosamine; it would be correct only if galactose addition were impaired.

options.text: H antigen
options.rationale: H substance is the core oligosaccharide present before A/B modifications; inability to add GalNAc does not remove the H substance itself.

options.text: Bombay phenotype
options.rationale: Bombay phenotype lacks H substance entirely; inability to add GalNAc produces type O phenotype if H is present, not Bombay.

options.text: AB antigen
options.rationale: AB requires both A and B terminal sugars; inability to add GalNAc would prevent A but could still allow B if galactose transferase is functional.

question: A researcher isolates a glycosaminoglycan composed of repeating disaccharide units of glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine linked β(1→3). Which mucopolysaccharide from the lecture matches this composition?
cited_learning_objective: Identify mucopolysaccharide structures and repeating disaccharide units

options.text: Hyaluronate (hyaluronic acid)
options.rationale: Lecture shows hyaluronate consists of repeating glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine linked β(1→3) and β(1→4) alternately; the β(1→3) linkage between these units is characteristic.

options.text: Heparin
options.rationale: Heparin contains iduronic acid and glucosamine with sulfation patterns; it would be correct only if the repeating units matched heparin's composition.

options.text: Chondroitin sulfate
options.rationale: Chondroitin sulfate is composed of glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine, not GlcNAc; it would be correct only if GalNAc were present instead of GlcNAc.

options.text: Dermatan sulfate
options.rationale: Dermatan sulfate contains iduronic acid and GalNAc variants; it would be correct only if iduronic acid replaced glucuronic acid.

options.text: Keratan sulfate
options.rationale: Keratan sulfate is composed of galactose and GlcNAc, not glucuronic acid; it would be correct only if galactose were the uronic sugar.

question: A patient with suspected glycogen storage disease has impaired debranching enzyme activity. Based on the lecture’s description of glycogen structure, which glycosidic bond would accumulate at branch points?
cited_learning_objective: Describe glycogen branching and α(1→6) linkages

options.text: α(1→6) glycosidic bonds at branch points
options.rationale: Lecture explains glycogen branching occurs via α(1→6) linkages; defective debranching would lead to accumulation of these branch point bonds.

options.text: α(1→4) glycosidic bonds in linear chains
options.rationale: α(1→4) bonds form the linear backbone and would accumulate only if chain elongation or cleavage of linear segments were impaired.

options.text: β(1→4) glycosidic bonds in structural fibers
options.rationale: β(1→4) bonds are characteristic of cellulose, not glycogen; it would be correct only if structural β linkages were involved.

options.text: β(1→3) glycosidic bonds in mucopolysaccharides
options.rationale: β(1→3) bonds occur in some GAGs; this would be correct only if glycogen used β linkages, which it does not.

options.text: α(1→2) glycosidic bonds between glucose and fructose
options.rationale: α(1→2) bonds are in sucrose (glucose–fructose), not glycogen; it would be correct only if sucrose-like linkages were present in glycogen.

question: A clinician considers enzyme replacement for a mucopolysaccharidosis caused by α-L-iduronidase deficiency. Which syndrome and primary accumulated substrates from the lecture would this therapy target?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss lysosomal storage disorders mucopolysaccharidoses and enzyme deficiencies

options.text: Hurler syndrome with heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate accumulation
options.rationale: Lecture identifies Hurler syndrome as α-L-iduronidase deficiency leading to accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfates; enzyme replacement would target these substrates.

options.text: Hunter syndrome with heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate accumulation
options.rationale: Hunter syndrome involves iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency (X-linked); enzyme replacement for α-L-iduronidase would not correct Hunter unless α-L-iduronidase were deficient.

options.text: Tay–Sachs disease with GM2 ganglioside accumulation
options.rationale: Tay–Sachs is due to hexosaminidase A deficiency causing GM2 accumulation; it would be correct only if the enzyme deficiency and substrates matched Tay–Sachs.

options.text: Niemann–Pick disease with sphingomyelin accumulation
options.rationale: Niemann–Pick involves sphingomyelinase deficiency and sphingomyelin accumulation; it would be correct only if the disorder and substrates matched.

options.text: Gaucher disease with glucocerebroside accumulation
options.rationale: Gaucher disease is due to glucocerebrosidase deficiency causing glucocerebroside buildup; it would be correct only if that enzyme were deficient.

question: A patient with chronic diarrhea is found to have bacterial overgrowth producing short-chain fatty acids from undigested carbohydrates. Which lecture-described carbohydrate modification would most directly prevent a monosaccharide from leaving the cell and thus reduce its availability for bacterial fermentation?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss phosphorylation of sugars and how it locks sugars inside the cell

options.text: Phosphorylation of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate
options.rationale: Lecture explains phosphorylation (e.g., glucose → G6P) prevents transporters from binding phosphorylated glucose, trapping it intracellularly and reducing luminal substrate for bacteria.

options.text: Acetylation of glucose to form N-acetylglucosamine
options.rationale: Acetylation produces amino sugars used in structural polymers, not a mechanism to trap free glucose intracellularly; it would be correct only if acetylation prevented export similarly to phosphorylation.

options.text: Glycosylation of proteins with O-linked GalNAc
options.rationale: O-glycosylation attaches sugars to proteins, not free monosaccharides; it would be correct only if glycosylation removed free sugars from the lumen.

options.text: Sulfation of glycosaminoglycans increasing their negative charge
options.rationale: Sulfation modifies GAGs for ECM function and does not trap free monosaccharides inside cells; it would be correct only if sulfation affected monosaccharide transport.

options.text: Branching of glycogen via α(1→6) linkages
options.rationale: Branching stores glucose as polymer but requires intracellular enzymatic steps; phosphorylation is the immediate trap—branching would be correct only if polymerization were the primary trapping step.

question: A patient with a rare mutation prevents formation of the anomeric carbon during sugar cyclization. Which property described in the lecture would be directly lost in the mutant monosaccharide?
cited_learning_objective: Explain cyclization of carbohydrates and the formation of anomeric carbons and anomers

options.text: Ability to form α and β anomers
options.rationale: Lecture explains cyclization creates a new asymmetric anomeric carbon that can exist as α or β; without cyclization, anomer formation is impossible.

options.text: Presence of a carbonyl group in the linear form
options.rationale: The carbonyl exists in the open-chain form prior to cyclization; loss of anomeric carbon formation would not remove the original carbonyl unless the molecule were altered.

options.text: Chirality at all original stereocenters
options.rationale: Cyclization creates an additional stereocenter but does not eliminate existing chiral centers; this would be correct only if original stereocenters were racemized.

options.text: Ability to be classified as an aldose or ketose
options.rationale: Aldose/ketose classification depends on the carbonyl position in the linear form and remains definable even without cyclization; it would be correct only if the carbonyl were absent.

options.text: Formation of epimers at C-4
options.rationale: Epimerization at C-4 is independent of anomer formation; loss of anomeric carbon would not prevent epimer differences at other carbons.

question: A patient with suspected congenital disorder of glycosylation has defective N-linked glycosylation. According to the lecture, which amino acid residue on proteins would most likely lack carbohydrate attachment?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss proteoglycan linkages and N-glycosidic bonds

options.text: Asparagine
options.rationale: Lecture states N-glycosidic bonds attach carbohydrates to the amide nitrogen of asparagine side chains; defective N-glycosylation would affect Asn-linked glycans.

options.text: Serine
options.rationale: Serine is the site of O-linked glycosylation; it would be correct only if O-glycosylation were defective rather than N-linked.

options.text: Threonine
options.rationale: Threonine is also an O-linked glycosylation site; it would be correct only if O-glycosylation were the affected pathway.

options.text: Lysine
options.rationale: Lysine is not the canonical N-linked glycosylation site; it would be correct only if an atypical glycosylation on lysine occurred.

options.text: Tyrosine
options.rationale: Tyrosine glycosylation is rare and not the primary N-linked site; it would be correct only in exceptional cases.

question: A patient with chronic hypercholesterolemia is advised that dietary fiber can help control cholesterol. Based on the lecture, which fiber property most directly contributes to cholesterol control?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss dietary fiber functions including cholesterol control

options.text: Indigestible fiber binds bile acids and reduces cholesterol reabsorption
options.rationale: Lecture lists fiber functions including control of cholesterol; insoluble and soluble fibers can bind bile acids, promoting excretion and lowering cholesterol.

options.text: Fiber increases pancreatic lipase activity enhancing cholesterol synthesis
options.rationale: Fiber does not increase pancreatic lipase to raise cholesterol; it would be correct only if fiber stimulated lipase and cholesterol production.

options.text: Fiber is absorbed and converted into HDL in the liver
options.rationale: Fiber is not absorbed and does not convert into HDL; this would be correct only if fiber were metabolized into lipoproteins.

options.text: Fiber directly inhibits HMG-CoA reductase in hepatocytes
options.rationale: Lecture does not state fiber inhibits HMG-CoA reductase; it would be correct only if fiber had a direct enzymatic inhibitory effect on cholesterol synthesis.

options.text: Fiber increases intestinal cholesterol synthesis increasing fecal cholesterol
options.rationale: Fiber reduces cholesterol absorption and increases excretion rather than increasing intestinal cholesterol synthesis; it would be correct only if synthesis were upregulated.

question: A patient with suspected deficiency of enzymes that remove sulfate groups from glycosaminoglycans presents with features overlapping Hurler syndrome. Which lecture-described enzyme deficiency would produce a similar mucopolysaccharide accumulation if sulfatase activity were lost?
cited_learning_objective: Relate specific enzyme defects to mucopolysaccharide accumulation and clinical syndromes

options.text: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency producing dermatan and heparan sulfate accumulation
options.rationale: Lecture identifies iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency as Hunter syndrome, leading to accumulation of heparan and dermatan sulfates; loss of sulfatase activity causes similar substrate buildup.

options.text: α-L-iduronidase deficiency producing keratan sulfate accumulation
options.rationale: α-L-iduronidase deficiency (Hurler) leads to heparan and dermatan sulfate accumulation, not keratan sulfate; it would be correct only if keratan sulfate were the primary substrate.

options.text: Arylsulfatase B deficiency producing glycosaminoglycan accumulation in cornea
options.rationale: Arylsulfatase B deficiency causes other mucopolysaccharidoses with different GAGs; it would be correct only if the clinical and substrate profile matched that enzyme's disease.

options.text: Hexosaminidase A deficiency producing heparan sulfate accumulation
options.rationale: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes GM2 ganglioside accumulation (Tay–Sachs), not heparan sulfate; it would be correct only if hexosaminidase targeted GAGs.

options.text: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency producing dermatan sulfate accumulation
options.rationale: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher) leads to glucocerebroside accumulation, not dermatan sulfate; it would be correct only if the enzyme acted on GAGs.

question: A newborn screen shows absent activity of an enzyme that normally cleaves β(1→4) linkages in bacterial peptidoglycan. Which innate immune enzyme from the lecture is likely deficient and what clinical consequence might follow?
cited_learning_objective: Explain lysozyme function and its role in innate immunity

options.text: Lysozyme deficiency; increased susceptibility to bacterial infections
options.rationale: Lecture describes lysozyme cleaving β(1→4) bonds in peptidoglycan; deficiency would impair this innate defense and increase infection risk.

options.text: Lactase deficiency; increased neonatal diarrhea from lactose malabsorption
options.rationale: Lactase acts on lactose in the gut, not peptidoglycan; this would be correct only if the enzyme measured were lactase and the clinical picture matched lactose intolerance.

options.text: Cellulase deficiency; failure to digest plant fiber leading to constipation
options.rationale: Cellulase digests cellulose and humans lack it normally; deficiency would not explain susceptibility to bacterial infection and would be correct only if fiber digestion were the issue.

options.text: Amylase deficiency; impaired starch digestion causing hypoglycemia
options.rationale: Amylase digests starch; its deficiency affects carbohydrate digestion, not innate bacterial cell wall cleavage; it would be correct only if starch digestion were implicated.

options.text: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency; accumulation of dermatan sulfate causing organomegaly
options.rationale: Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency causes Hunter syndrome with organomegaly, not innate immune impairment; it would be correct only if mucopolysaccharide storage were the primary concern.

question: A patient with suspected congenital absence of the enzyme that converts glucose to glucose-6-phosphate is studied. According to the lecture, which immediate cellular effect would most likely be observed?
cited_learning_objective: Describe phosphorylation of sugars and consequences for cellular glucose handling

options.text: Inability to trap glucose intracellularly leading to impaired glycolysis
options.rationale: Lecture explains phosphorylation (to G6P) locks glucose inside the cell and is the first step of glycolysis; absence would prevent trapping and impair glycolysis.

options.text: Excess glycogen branching due to unregulated α(1→6) linkages
options.rationale: Glycogen branching depends on branching enzymes and available G6P; without phosphorylation, glycogen synthesis would be reduced, not increased.

options.text: Accumulation of free phosphorylated sugars in the cytosol
options.rationale: If phosphorylation is absent, phosphorylated sugars would not accumulate; this would be correct only if downstream dephosphorylation were blocked.

options.text: Increased export of glucose due to enhanced transporter affinity for G6P
options.rationale: Transporters do not bind phosphorylated glucose; absence of phosphorylation would increase export, not enhanced affinity for G6P; this would be correct only if transporters recognized G6P.

options.text: Enhanced formation of N-acetylglucosamine from glucose increasing structural polymers
options.rationale: Conversion to GlcNAc requires specific pathways and acetylation; lack of phosphorylation would not directly enhance GlcNAc formation and polymerization.

question: A patient with chronic constipation is counseled about fiber types. According to the lecture, which of the following is a correct pairing of fiber property and physiologic benefit?
cited_learning_objective: List the functions of dietary fiber including bowel health and weight control

options.text: Indigestible fiber increases stool bulk and helps maintain bowel regularity
options.rationale: Lecture lists dietary fiber (indigestible cellulose) as normalizing bowel movements and maintaining bowel health by acting as a bulking agent.

options.text: Indigestible fiber is absorbed and increases blood glucose rapidly
options.rationale: Indigestible fiber is not absorbed and does not raise blood glucose; this would be correct only if the fiber were digestible carbohydrate.

options.text: Soluble fiber is converted to cholesterol in the liver increasing LDL
options.rationale: Soluble fiber tends to lower cholesterol by binding bile acids; it would be correct only if fiber increased hepatic cholesterol synthesis leading to higher LDL.

options.text: Insoluble fiber decreases stool bulk and causes constipation
options.rationale: Insoluble fiber increases stool bulk and relieves constipation; this would be correct only if fiber reduced bulk, which contradicts the lecture.

options.text: Dietary fiber directly supplies ATP to colonocytes via absorption
options.rationale: Fiber itself is not absorbed to supply ATP; fermentation products (SCFAs) can be used by colonocytes, but fiber is not directly absorbed as ATP source.

question: A patient with a mutation preventing formation of N-acetylneuraminic acid on leukocyte glycoproteins is studied. Based on the lecture, which leukocyte function would be impaired?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the role of sialic acid in leukocyte rolling and selectin binding

options.text: Leukocyte rolling mediated by selectin binding
options.rationale: Lecture states selectins bind sialic acid residues on glycoproteins to mediate leukocyte rolling; absence of sialic acid would impair this interaction.

options.text: Phagocytosis via Fc receptor recognition
options.rationale: Fc receptor–mediated phagocytosis depends on antibody opsonization, not sialic acid; it would be correct only if sialylation directly affected Fc binding.

options.text: Oxidative burst due to NADPH oxidase activation
options.rationale: Oxidative burst is intracellular and not directly dependent on surface sialic acid; it would be correct only if sialic acid regulated NADPH oxidase.

options.text: Complement C3b deposition on bacterial surfaces
options.rationale: Complement deposition is a separate pathway and not directly mediated by leukocyte sialic acid; it would be correct only if sialic acid influenced complement activation.

options.text: Chemotaxis toward IL-8 gradients
options.rationale: Chemotaxis relies on chemokine receptors and intracellular signaling, not sialic acid–selectin interactions; it would be correct only if sialic acid affected chemokine receptor function.

question: A patient with suspected deficiency of brush-border disaccharidases cannot digest sucrose. According to the lecture, which enzyme is most likely deficient and what bond does it cleave?
cited_learning_objective: List disaccharide-specific enzymes and the bonds they hydrolyze

options.text: Sucrase; cleaves α(1→2) bond in sucrose
options.rationale: Lecture states sucrose (glucose–fructose) is hydrolyzed by sucrase at the α(1→2) linkage.

options.text: Lactase; cleaves β(1→4) bond in lactose
options.rationale: Lactase cleaves lactose β(1→4) bonds; it would be correct only if the disaccharide were lactose.

options.text: Maltase; cleaves β(1→4) bond in maltose
options.rationale: Maltase cleaves α(1→4) bonds in maltose, not β(1→4); this would be correct only if maltose had β linkages.

options.text: Isomaltase; cleaves β(1→6) branch points in glycogen
options.rationale: Isomaltase acts on α(1→6) branch points, not β(1→6); it would be correct only if branch point linkages were β and in glycogen.

options.text: Cellulase; cleaves β(1→4) bonds in cellulose
options.rationale: Cellulase cleaves β(1→4) cellulose bonds and humans lack it; it would be correct only if sucrose contained β(1→4) cellulose-like bonds.

question: A patient with a rare mutation prevents addition of fucose to the H substance. According to the lecture, which blood group antigen would be absent or altered in this patient?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the H substance composition and its role in blood group antigen formation

options.text: All ABO antigens would be absent (Bombay phenotype)
options.rationale: Lecture indicates the H substance includes fucose; absence of fucosylation prevents formation of H substance and thus A/B antigens, producing the Bombay phenotype.

options.text: Only A antigen would be absent while B remains
options.rationale: A antigen requires GalNAc addition to H substance; if H is absent due to lack of fucose, both A and B cannot form, so this would be correct only if fucose were required only for A.

options.text: Only B antigen would be absent while A remains
options.rationale: B antigen requires galactose addition to H substance; absence of fucose prevents H formation for both A and B, so this would be correct only if B formation were independent of fucose.

options.text: Type O blood would be converted to type A
options.rationale: Type O has H substance but lacks A/B terminal sugars; without fucose, H is absent and the phenotype is Bombay, not conversion to A.

options.text: Type AB would become type B due to loss of GalNAc transferase
options.rationale: Loss of fucose affects H substance, not GalNAc transferase; this would be correct only if the A transferase were specifically lost.

question: A patient with chronic sinus infections is found to have defective sialylation of mucins in airway secretions. Based on the lecture, which mucin property and function would be most directly affected?
cited_learning_objective: Explain mucin composition and the role of sialic acid in mucosal glycoproteins

options.text: Negative charge and binding interactions of mucins reducing pathogen clearance
options.rationale: Lecture notes mucins often contain sialic acid; loss of sialylation reduces negative charge and selectin/sialic acid–mediated interactions, impairing mucosal defense and clearance.

options.text: Proteolytic stability of mucin peptide backbone increasing degradation
options.rationale: Sialylation primarily affects glycan charge and recognition, not direct proteolytic stability of the peptide backbone; this would be correct only if sialic acid protected against proteases.

options.text: Ability of mucins to form N-glycosidic bonds to asparagine
options.rationale: Mucin O-glycosylation involves Ser/Thr and GalNAc; sialylation does not determine N-glycosylation to Asn, so this would be correct only if N-glycosylation were dependent on sialic acid.

options.text: Conversion of mucins into glycosaminoglycans increasing viscosity
options.rationale: Mucins and GAGs are distinct classes; loss of sialylation does not convert mucins into GAGs, so this would be correct only if biochemical pathways were altered.

options.text: Direct inhibition of Na+/K+ ATPase in airway epithelial cells
options.rationale: Sialylation of mucins does not directly inhibit Na+/K+ ATPase; this would be correct only if sialic acid acted as an ATPase inhibitor.
